title: The Importance Ratio Was Living at the Wrong Scale: GSPO and What It Taught Us About GRPO

body:
A year and a half ago, GRPO looked like the final word on critic-free policy optimization for reasoning models. DeepSeekMath proposed it, DeepSeek-R1 proved it, and dozens of papers mimicked it. The idea was clean: estimate the advantage from a group of sampled completions by subtracting the group mean and dividing by the group standard deviation, so you no longer need a learned value network. In practice it works. In practice it also breaks, and the way it breaks tells you something general about where variance-reduction tricks come from and what they cost.

The symptom shows up most clearly in mixture-of-experts models. Train a dense 7B reasoning model with GRPO and the loss descends. Scale up to a 100B+ parameter MoE and training stalls, oscillates, or diverges. Alibaba's Qwen team called this out in July 2025 and proposed a one-line change: do not take the importance ratio token by token; take it over the whole sequence. The resulting method, Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), has in a few months become the default for frontier MoE reasoning training. The reason is a lesson that extends well past this particular method.

## Why this matters

GRPO's descent from PPO reused an object that PPO was always slightly uncomfortable with: the per-token importance ratio $r_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(o_t \mid x, o_{<t}) / \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_t \mid x, o_{<t})$. In a short conversational response that ratio is close to one and life is calm. In a 10,000-token chain of thought drawn from a sparse MoE, the policy at step $t$ has been routed through a different combination of experts than the old policy was, and $r_t$ can swing by orders of magnitude. Clipping at $1 \pm 0.2$ hides some of the pathology; what leaks through becomes the gradient. The gradient becomes a lottery.

The practical story in the GSPO paper is that the Qwen team had to maintain a parallel infrastructure called *Routing Replay* — recording which experts fired for each token under the old policy and forcing the same routing under the new one — just to keep GRPO stable on their large MoE runs. That infrastructure cost memory, communication, and model capacity, and it was fragile. GSPO's single reframing eliminated the need for it. The result is not just a cleaner algorithm but a case study in what the right unit of accounting looks like in a model whose compute path is itself stochastic.

## The core idea

Fix a question $x$ and sample $G$ responses $\{y_1, \ldots, y_G\}$ from the old policy $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$. Each response is a token sequence $y_i = (y_{i,1}, \ldots, y_{i, |y_i|})$ with a scalar reward $R(x, y_i)$ (a verifier flag, a human preference score, whatever). Compute the group-normalized advantage

$$
A_i \;=\; \frac{R(x, y_i) - \mathrm{mean}_{j}\, R(x, y_j)}{\mathrm{std}_{j}\, R(x, y_j)}.
$$

Every token in $y_i$ inherits the same scalar $A_i$. This is the GRPO baseline, and it is the shared piece.

The two methods differ in how they translate advantage into a policy update. GRPO forms a per-token clipped surrogate

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|} \min\!\Big( r_{i,t}(\theta)\, A_i,\; \mathrm{clip}(r_{i,t}(\theta), 1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon)\, A_i \Big),
$$

with $r_{i,t}(\theta) = \pi_\theta(y_{i,t} \mid x, y_{i, <t}) / \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i,t} \mid x, y_{i, <t})$ clipped per token. GSPO replaces this with a sequence-level ratio

$$
s_i(\theta) \;=\; \left(\frac{\pi_\theta(y_i \mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_i \mid x)}\right)^{1/|y_i|} \;=\; \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|} \log r_{i,t}(\theta)\right)
$$

and clips once per response:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{GSPO}}(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G} \min\!\Big( s_i(\theta)\, A_i,\; \mathrm{clip}(s_i(\theta), 1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon)\, A_i \Big).
$$

The length-normalising exponent is the quiet move. Without it, long sequences would dominate numerically; with it, $s_i$ is the geometric mean of the per-token ratios. A single wild token no longer carries the whole response's update, and a response's clip decision is made once, from a stabilised statistic, rather than $|y_i|$ times from noisy ones.

Two consequences follow. First, the gradient contribution of a response is binary at the sequence level: either the clip does not bite and all of $y_i$ gets a uniform $A_i$-weighted push, or the clip bites and $y_i$ is dropped from the update entirely. Second, when the model is MoE, the per-token ratios still fluctuate — different experts fire for the same token under $\theta$ and $\theta_{\text{old}}$ — but the geometric mean dampens outliers. The paper argues that even if roughly 10% of tokens cross expert boundaries between the old and new policy, the sequence-level ratio moves modestly, and routing replay becomes unnecessary.

## A concrete anchor

Set $G = 4$ responses of length $|y_i| = 1000$, with per-token log-ratios $\log r_{i,t}$ drawn independently from a mean-zero distribution with standard deviation $\sigma$. The per-token ratio has variance $\exp(\sigma^2) - 1$ for log-normal factors. The sequence-level log-ratio is $(1/|y_i|) \sum_t \log r_{i,t}$, which by independence has standard deviation $\sigma / \sqrt{|y_i|} \approx \sigma/31.6$. Suppose $\sigma = 0.5$ at the token scale — not unusual for an MoE whose routing has mildly shifted. The per-token ratio spread then spans roughly $e^{\pm 1} \approx [0.37, 2.72]$, so the per-token clip bites on perhaps a tenth of the tokens of every response. The sequence-level ratio spans $e^{\pm 0.03} \approx [0.97, 1.03]$: the sequence-level clip rarely fires. Variance reduction here is the dilution of thousands of noisy observations into one stable one. It costs you token-level resolution. GRPO was spending that resolution on noise anyway.

The second thing to notice in this toy is what happens as $\sigma$ grows. In a dense model with a stable per-token distribution, $\sigma \sim 0.05$ or so, and both methods look identical in expectation — GSPO's variance reduction buys very little, and GRPO's token-level resolution is informative. In a large MoE where routing drift pushes $\sigma$ past $0.3$, GRPO degrades fast while GSPO barely moves. The two methods are not uniformly ranked; which one is correct depends on where the per-token ratio distribution actually lives. The published MoE training curves (Qwen3 series, July 2025) show the crossover clearly.

A short PyTorch sketch for the sequence-level ratio and clip, assuming per-token log-probabilities under both policies:

```python
# logp_new, logp_old: (B, T) summed only where mask == 1
# mask: (B, T) ignores pad tokens
seq_len = mask.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1)
seq_log_ratio = ((logp_new - logp_old) * mask).sum(dim=1) / seq_len
s = torch.exp(seq_log_ratio.detach() + (seq_log_ratio - seq_log_ratio.detach()))
# unclipped and clipped surrogate
surr_unclip = s * advantage
surr_clip = torch.clamp(s, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * advantage
loss = -torch.min(surr_unclip, surr_clip).mean()
```

The straight-through construction of `s` is standard: autograd sees the sequence-level log-ratio but the forward value is the ratio itself.

## What it implies in practice

Three handles. First, if you are training an MoE reasoning model with GRPO and your loss curves wobble — spikes without obvious reward correlate, slow drift in token-length statistics, or a sudden fraction of batches where every response is clipped — inspect the per-token importance-ratio histogram across a batch rather than reaching for Routing Replay. If the tails are heavy, GSPO's one-line change may absorb the instability. Second, if you are already on GSPO and you see a different pathology — short responses dominating, or a benchmark where response length collapses after a few hundred steps — you have found the known failure mode: because the whole response is clipped as one object, GSPO can bias the policy toward responses whose length falls inside the clipping sweet spot. The length-unbiased variants that have appeared since are a reaction to this. Third, when designing any variance-reduction scheme over a sequence model with stochastic routing, ask what statistic is actually trustworthy at the scale the gradient is being computed. In MoE, per-token ratios are not that statistic. In dense models with coherent per-token semantics, they often are. The general lesson is older than GSPO: a variance-reduction technique is a choice about what to average over, and that choice should match the scale at which your noise lives.

## Limits and open questions

GSPO is not final. The claim that sequence-level clipping removes MoE routing instability has been partly contested in work from late 2025. *Towards Stable and Effective Reinforcement Learning for Mixture-of-Experts* (RSPO) reports that under heavy router shift GSPO still exhibits bursty clipping and training collapse, and proposes a per-token router-shift ratio that down-weights tokens with large routing deviations before the surrogate is formed. A separate line attributes most MoE RL instability to rollout–training routing mismatch between inference and training engines, where the hardware kernels diverge in their routing even for the same input, and proposes a *Rollout Routing Replay* to record and reuse inference-time routing — a variant of the mechanism GSPO's authors claimed to retire, re-introduced for a slightly different reason. The upshot is that "routing instability" is at least two problems wearing one name: a statistical instability in the importance ratio that GSPO solves, and a numerical mismatch between serving and training engines that it does not.

A short analysis titled *Rethinking GSPO: The Perplexity-Entropy Equivalence* observes that the length-normalised log-ratio is numerically close to a per-token entropy signal, which both explains why the method stabilises training — it tracks a smooth, interpretable quantity — and suggests cheaper proxies that avoid the ratio altogether. On the GSPO side, length-unbiased variants have begun to appear, with the common goal of decoupling the clipping decision from the response length while keeping the sequence-level stabilisation.

The broader open question is methodological. Comparative studies on the DAPO–GRPO–GSPO axis report that the choice of surrogate accounts for less of the final benchmark gap than the choice of reward shaping, sampling discipline, and training data mix. That is useful context: a cleaner objective is not a substitute for a cleaner training recipe. The surrogate is one knob of several, and the field is still learning which knob is which. For the reader, the pragmatic reading is to treat the GRPO–GSPO choice as an architecture-conditioned decision, not a universal upgrade — and to measure, on your own curves, whether the surrogate you picked is where your run is actually losing information.

## Further reading

- Shao, Z. et al. (2024). *DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models.* arXiv:2402.03300. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300>. The original GRPO proposal; worth re-reading now that follow-ups have teased apart which of its design choices actually matter.
- Zheng, C. et al. (2025). *Group Sequence Policy Optimization.* arXiv:2507.18071. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071>. The GSPO paper. The derivation of the sequence-level ratio and the MoE stability argument are the two pieces to read.
- Yu, Q. et al. (2025). *DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale.* arXiv:2503.14476. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476>. The complementary line: fix GRPO through asymmetric clipping and dynamic sampling rather than by changing the ratio's unit. Worth comparing head-to-head with GSPO.
- *Rethinking GSPO: The Perplexity-Entropy Equivalence* (2025). arXiv:2510.23142. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23142>. A short analytical note that shows the length-normalised log-ratio is close to a per-token entropy, which helps intuition and suggests cheaper surrogates.
- *Towards Stable and Effective Reinforcement Learning for Mixture-of-Experts* (RSPO, 2025). arXiv:2510.23027. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23027>. Pushback: GSPO alone does not solve router-shift instability; a per-token router-shift ratio is proposed on top.
- *Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers* (2025). arXiv:2510.11370. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370>. Attributes MoE RL instability to the routing mismatch between rollout and training engines, and proposes Rollout Routing Replay as a mitigation.
